BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Drying conditions and near normal temperatures will return for the weekend thanks to a building ridge of high pressure over the West Coast.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A chance of showers will spread northward into the area tonight, then become widespread Thursday and Thursday night. There is a slight chance of thunderstorms this afternoon/evening, then a better chance Thursday afternoon and evening.
- Thunderstorms Thursday afternoon into evening will be capable of isolated severe wind gusts/hail in Southwest Idaho.
- Becoming windy late Thursday night behind a cold front, with much cooler conditions Friday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Light showers with some embedded thunder have been ongoing overnight over SW Idaho as southerly flow aloft has continued to push moisture into the area. Despite the moisture, the area today will see minimal precipitation chances until evening. Models have been increasing in confidence about a dry slot moving overhead through the afternoon, clearing skies and keeping precipitation chances primarily to the west-central Idaho mountains and south- central Idaho. Even then, chances only range from 10-15%. If a stray shower or thunderstorm were to emerge, the primary threat would be localized heavy rainfall, with a secondary threat of gusty outflow winds. Otherwise, through the day today, warm conditions can be expected.

Once this evening/overnight rolls around, the low pressure system will begin to move onshore into California and Nevada. Precipitation chances will steadily rise in SE Oregon through the night, with high confidence in a band of precipitation moving from south-to-north. Embedded thunderstorms are possible as this band moves north overnight at 10-15% chances. SW Idaho precipitation chances start to increase late morning into the afternoon as the system moves into northern Nevada. Widespread rain and scattered embedded thunderstorms are forecast Thursday and Thursday night, especially on the SW Idaho side. Upwards of 30% chances for thunderstorms are forecast, highest in south- central Idaho and the western Magic Valley. Favorable convective parameters in this area, including MLCAPE near 500 J/kg and effective shear values 20-25 kts, will enable multicell clusters and transient supercells. The primary threat will be outflow wind gusts up to 50 mph, with a secondary threat of hail. The time frame of this threat will begin Thursday afternoon and taper off by evening.

The QPF totals are indicative of the high PWAT values, showing event totals of 0.30 to 0.50 inches in the Treasure and Magic Valleys, and 0.60 to 1.00 inches at higher elevations. Less rain will fall in Oregon on the western flank of the upper low. That area will have 0.20 to 0.30 inches in the valleys and up to 0.70 inches at higher elevations and/or closer to the ID border. Higher totals will be seen where thunderstorms cores move over. With flow aloft continuing from the south through this event, snow levels will remain above 9000 feet, so all precipitation will be rain.

The upper-level low will move overhead Thursday night into Friday, then gradually NE of the area through Friday night. Flow aloft will shift out of the NW, with a cold front moving through Thursday night. Pre-frontal winds will increase out of the SE through the western Snake plain Thursday afternoon, then shift to gusty northwest late Thursday night behind the cold front. Snow levels will lower by Friday afternoon, down to around 5000-7000 ft MSL. Higher elevation passes and ridgetops will likely only see a dusting of snow as precipitation chances gradually taper off west-to-east behind the front. Gusts up of 30-40 mph will be seen across the area, excluding sheltered mountain valleys. The highest speeds will be seen across higher terrain, ridgetops, and south/east of Boise through the western Magic Valley. Once the winds taper off Friday night, valley floors are forecast to cool down into the low-to-mid 30s. Areas of fog will form Friday morning in the wetter and wind- protected northern valleys and again late Friday night.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Drying conditions and near normal temperatures will return for the weekend thanks to a building ridge of high pressure over the West Coast. By late Sunday, long range forecast models have once again converged on a closed low pressure system moving onshore and slowly east over the area through the early part of next week. This pattern would bring cooler and wetter conditions yet again by early next week. The highest chances for precipitation would be over the west-central Idaho mountains. With how highly variable and volatile the synoptic pattern has been even just within 24 hours of this forecast, forecaster confidence is low at this time.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: Long range models start to disagree at the beginning of the work week, with the GFS suggesting a strong upper-level low diving southward out of Canada into the northwestern CONUS.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Above average temperatures will continue through the end of the week, but a weekend system will drop temperatures towards near- to below-average temperatures.
- Precipitation possible Friday through Sunday, with the potential for frozen precipitation outside of the mountain on Sunday.
- Another system will try to take shape for mid-week, with the potential for additional precipitation and, possibly, high winds.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Mostly clear skies ongoing tonight across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. A few mid-level clouds are visible on satellite drifting across Niobrara County with some lower clouds over Carbon, Sioux, and Dawes counties. Winds are mostly light tonight outside of Bordeaux with temperatures in the mid-40s and low-50s area-wide. High-level clouds are starting to surge up from the southeast and are moving into Wyoming from Utah and Colorado. These high clouds will continue to push into western portions of the CWA before spreading eastward throughout the morning and afternoon hours.

Upper-level flow today will remain benign as an upper-level ridge continues to develop across the central CONUS. Southwesterly flow will continue across the CWA in the upper-level with the building ridge. An upper-level low will start to move inland into southern California during the day, with a stout jet developing. A 500mb shortwave look to develop and push across western portions of the CWA this evening, leading to a brief 3 to 6 hour period of enhanced, dynamic lift. Strong 500mb CVA will help eject this shortwave through quickly, leading to minimal precipitation chances for most areas. 700mb flow remains fairly weak from the southwest, though a 700mb shortwave develops with the 500mb shortwave moving through. With southwesterly upper-level flow, moisture from the Pacific Ocean will advect into the Intermountain West, leading to increased moisture mostly west of the Laramie Range in southeast Wyoming. As a result, with the 500mb and 700mb shortwave pushing through this evening, a few showers may develop along the Sierra Madre Range this evening, especially as surface flow turns southwesterly. 700mb temperatures will remain quite warm this evening, in the 4 to 5C range across Carbon County, which will prevent any frozen precipitation from developing along the Sierra Madre Range. Significant precipitation is not expected today, with total accumulations remaining around a trace for a small portion of Carbon County. Temperatures will be well above average once again today, with highs in the mid-60s to mid-70s, with normal values for this time of year around the mid-50s to mid-60s.

Thursday will start to become more active as the upper-level low over western California moves east-northeastward inland towards the Intermountain West, ending around northern Nevada by Friday morning. The upper-level will be pushed off to the east as the low moves east- northeastward, with upper-level flow remaining southwesterly and increasing across southeast Wyoming and western Nebraska. Several lobes of 500mb vorticity will eject northeastward from the base of the upper-level trough, leading to increased synoptic ascent. The best forcing looks to, once again, remain confined to Carbon County and areas west of the Laramie Range for Thursday, but this will change for Friday and the weekend. 700mb flow starts to become more active as the shortwave ejects northeastward towards South Dakota and the winds begin to increase with the approaching system. Strong, southerly flow develops ahead of the approaching system by the afternoon hours, with flow increasing through the overnight hours. 700mb temperatures will remain quite warm, in the 7 to 9C range, for much of the area, therefore, any precipitation that falls will continue to be rain. Precipitation chances across Carbon and Albany counties will start to increase early Thursday morning and continuing through the evening hours. Precipitation looks to remain confined to west of the Laramie Range, where the best ascent and moisture will be located due to the southwesterly flow advecting in Pacific moisture and getting trapped along the Laramie Range. There will be meager CAPE across this region, so a rumble or two or thunder cannot be completely ruled out, though widespread storms are not expected. Temperatures will be above average again Thursday with highs in the low-60s to mid-70s, though overnight lows in the Sierra Madres may favor some flurries developing with the increased ascent and moisture in this region. Significant snowfall is not anticipated at this time for Thursday and Friday morning.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Active weather continues for Friday as the upper-level low across northern Nevada continues to push eastwards towards western Wyoming. A fairly strong, southerly, upper-level jet starts to move overhead Friday morning as the upper-level low pushes into Utah. With much of the region downstream of the upper-level trough axis and portions of the CWA within the left exit region of the jet, synoptic forcing will increase significantly from previous days. The trough starts to elongate overnight Friday, per the GFS and ECMWF, with the upper- level jet strengthening to around 100kts by Saturday morning. Unfortunately, very strong 500mb cyclonic vorticity advection (CVA) will develop across Montana, favoring the deepening of the northern portion of the system. This will lead to split flow developing across the Intermountain west, with the northern branch remaining much stronger than the southern branch. The southern branch looks to be the primary forcing mechanism for precipitation, so as this start to weaken, precipitation will decrease across the region. Similarly, the 700mb low will develop Friday morning before pushing northeastward and starting to elongate with the upper-level system. This will, once again, push the best forcing off the north with more modest forcing expected across the CWA and very weak 700mb flow developing for Saturday morning. Despite the less favorable evolution of this system, precipitation chances are expected to increase from southwest to northeast across the CWA Friday morning through Friday evening. Precipitation will remain mostly rain as 700mb temperatures stay fairly warm in the 5 to 8C range Friday evening. A strong cold front will accompany this system and will drop 700mb temperatures into the 0 to 4C range by early Saturday morning. With cooling temperatures at 700mb, rain across the Sierra Madre and Snowy ranges should change over to mostly snow overnight Friday into Saturday morning. Significant snow accumulation is not anticipated at this time, due to the weakening southern branch of the system. Temperatures will max out in the upper-50s to low-80s Friday afternoon, with the warmest temperatures across the western Nebraska Panhandle due to very strong southerly flow. Overnight lows will be much cooler, thanks to the incoming cold front, dropping into the mid-30s to low-50s everywhere.

Saturday turns much cooler as the cold front associated with the upper-level system moves through the region by mid-day Saturday, though daytime high temperatures will remain in the mid-40s to mid- 50s everywhere. Upper-level flow remains southerly across the CWA Saturday as the upper-level low slowly pushes eastward. Some synoptic ascent will be present Saturday as a few 500mb vorticity lobes eject northeastward and the region remains downstream of the trough axis, though this ascent will be weaker as the elongates southward. Weak, southerly to southeasterly 700mb flow is expected throughout the day Saturday as the 700mb flow get absorbed. 700mb temperatures will hover in the 0 to 2C range, with a few areas expected to see 700mb temperatures drop below 0C. Precipitation chances will decrease throughout the day Saturday as the best forcing weakens and moves away. Despite this, long range models are starting to suggest that a surface low will develop over southeastern Colorado Saturday evening into the early morning hours Sunday. Precipitation associated with this potential system would eject northeastward towards the CWA and collide with the backdoor cold front expected to swing into the region Saturday evening into the overnight hours. This collision could result in a favorable area for precipitation to develop across much of the CWA, especially western Nebraska.

On Sunday, the upper-level low is progged to get absorbed into the upper-level flow and finally push the upper-level trough through the Intermountain West by Monday morning. The backdoor, 700mb cold front looks to push through the Sunday morning hours, dropping 700mb temperatures to between -2 and 0C throughout the day Sunday. With the cold front potentially still colliding with the moisture push from the surface low across southeastern Colorado, precipitation chances may remain in place across the region. However, with 700mb temperatures currently progged to be between -2 and 0C, precipitation could change over to snow for much of the area, but especially southeast Wyoming along and east of the Laramie Range. There is still some uncertainty in this, though long range models remain in fairly good agreement on the propagation of this system. If this hold together, snow flurries could be flying across much of the CWA Sunday, though ground temperatures will likely remain too warm for accumulating snowfall.

Long range models start to disagree at the beginning of the work week, with the GFS suggesting a strong upper-level low diving southward out of Canada into the northwestern CONUS. The GFS suggest this low strengthening and moving west to east across Montana, leading to a 250mb, westerly jet around 100kts across the CWA by midweek. The ECMWF suggests a similar evolution though slower and a touch weaker than the GFS solution, with a broader upper-level trough compared to the amplified upper-level low in the GFS. The 700mb flow follows a similar pattern in the long range models, suggesting a westerly, low-level jet across the CWA by mid-week. This could result in a high wind event for some of the wind prone regions by Wednesday, but confidence is low at this time.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: Chances for light precipitation (valley rain, mountain snow above 10,000 feet) continue through the weekend as a low pressure system, currently spinning off the California coast, traverses the Intermountain West.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread rain is expected tomorrow through early Friday.
- Strong to severe storms will be possible near the Four Corners...favoring southeast Utah...on Wednesday and Thursday.
- The potential for flooding increases Thursday and Friday, especially for portions of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado.
- Rainfall amounts in the southern mountains range from 1-3 inches with higher amounts of 2-4" or more possible in the San Juans and southern foothills.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: HAZARDOUS WEATHER POSSIBLE THROUGH FRIDAY:

Remnant tropical moisture will once again take aim at the Intermountain West and Rockies. The first wave of this deeper moisture arrives to the Four Corners region by sunrise and track northeastward across the remainder of eastern Utah and western Colorado through the day before being swept away on Friday. A full array of hazards are possible with this prolonged event including river flooding, flash flooding, strong to severe thunderstorms, and snow above 12,000-13,000 feet. A Flood watch has been issued for parts of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado beginning 12 PM tomorrow and persisting through 12 PM Friday.

The 21/00Z KGJT RAOB is sitting at 2/3 of an inch of PWAT which is already anomalous and in the 90th percentile. Impressive for mid October but just the tip of the iceberg. GOES All Layer PWAT imagery is showing the nose of true tropical mositure moving into south-central AZ this evening and should arrive to the 4 Corners in the pre-sunrise hours. PWAT is projected to push above an inch by sunset at GJT which would be a new daily record and some 300+ percent of normal. So the stage will once again be set for excessive rainfall rates and impressive total precipitation amounts through the event. This moisture will also effectively lighten and destabilize the atmosphere and allow even minimal lift to produce ascent and efficiently squeeze out this anomalous PWAT. Ascent over the next few days will aided by a strong SubTrop jet aloft tomorrow followed by the Polar jet on Thursday which is associated with the main upstream trough over the West. CAPE will be modest at best over the 4 Corners region the next few afternoons. The wind profile will however be impressive...with low level east/southeast flow over-topped by the strong southwest flow aloft. This shear will be favorable for producing periods of organized convection even though plenty of cloud cover will inhibit full surface heating. Strong outflow winds will remain the main threat but some storms will also be capable of producing larger hail. The veering profile and local terrain effects could also lead to some brief spin ups...not probable but not zero either. Lastly the CAPE profile will be long and skinny...an indication of deep warm cloud processes which favor high precipitation rates as well as high snow levels. It should be no surprise that the fertile crescent of the San Juans will also be effective at producing the ascent in this southerly flow pattern. With the fire hose pointed directly at them precipitation amounts in the 2-4 inch range are still forecast with higher amounts possible due to convection. Rain or a nighttime mix at pass level could translate to 6 to 12 inches or more of snow over the highest peaks.

Unlike the last event the upstream system will be lifting northward through the Great Basin instead of sending the main circulation overhead. Drier air will be pulled in as this system lifts into the northern Rockies through the day on Friday. A decrease in precipitation coverage and intensity is expected through the day as PWAT is forecast to crash below a half of an inch by midday. Even after it stops raining, the risk for flooding will remain elevated on Friday as water continues to work through the system. Some main stem rivers are forecast to crest on Friday morning. We'll have a better idea of how long flooding may continue to cause issues after we get a better sense of how much rainfall is received on Thursday.

Chances for light precipitation (valley rain, mountain snow above 10,000 feet) continue through the weekend as a low pressure system, currently spinning off the California coast, traverses the Intermountain West. Plenty of uncertainty remains in how this low will evolve as it moves inland, but ensemble guidance tends to show a weakening system by the time it reaches our forecast area. Regardless, this system will provide enough forcing for scattered to widespread precipitation as it moves through, alongside a brief reduction in temperatures.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Saturday through Tuesday...While one low center lingers across the Four Corners, the northern piece cross the northern Rockies and pushes a cold front south into eastern CO Saturday morning.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Flood Watch in effect from this afternoon through Friday afternoon for the eastern San Juan mountains and the Upper Rio Grande Valley.
- Periods of moderate to heavy rain for the Continental Divide, focusing on the San Juan Range starting this afternoon and lasting through Friday, with the heaviest amounts forecast for Thursday.
- Heavy rain on top of saturated soils and higher elevation snow already in place will bring the threat of flooding, with rock/mud slides also possible along the Continental Divide.
- Generally warm and dry across the plains through Friday, then much cooler and unsettled starting Saturday.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Currently...Strong Pacific low centered off the CA coast was producing southwest flow across the Desert SW and the Four Corners overnight with just a few clouds pushing into the southwestern quad of CO. Otherwise, a mostly clear night with low temps expected to dip into the 30s for the high valleys, and 40s across the plains.

Today and tonight...Pacific low will linger off the CA coast through the day today, keeping a steady, moist southwest flow in place across the Four Corners, feeding moisture into western CO. At the same time, an upper ridge over the central US, with the ridge axis positioned over eastern CO, will help keep the plains warm and dry. Models indicate that the low center will finally push onshore overnight tonight. This timing seems to be slightly slower than previous runs, meaning that shower activity holds off on pushing across the Continental Divide until midday, then gradually increases in areal coverage and intensity through the afternoon and evening. This slower progression seems to keep CAPE somewhat subdued, so even though showers and some storms are anticipated, just general thunder is expected. As for QPF amounts through the first 24 hours, plan on a few tenths along the Continental Divide, with up to around .6 of an inch across the favored SW mts. Flood Watch remains in effect starting this afternoon through Friday afternoon. Look for high temps today in the 60s across the high valleys and 70s for the plains. Increasing sw flow, coupled with moisture advection and increasing clouds, should keep overnight lows a bit more mild, with temps bottoming out in the 40s for the high valleys, and mid 40s to mid 50s for the plains.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Thursday...All indications point to Thursday as seeing the greatest impacts from this Pacific storm. As the low continues moving east across CA and NV through the day, an upper shortwave rotates across AZ and into the Four Corners region. This upper support, coupled with increasing proximity of the system, will mean periods of heavy rainfall across western CO and along the Continental Divide through the entire day. The focus area continues to be the southwest mts, with total additional rainfall amounts ranging from an inch up to 2.75 inches possible through the day, while the remainder of the higher terrain could see around half an inch. SPC shows the Marginal area for strong to severe thunderstorms creeping into the southwestern corner of the state, giving a nod to the abundant moisture plus upper level support, so periods of heavy convective rainfall falling on already saturated ground and some high elevation snow pack leading to excessive runoff will be possible, hence the ongoing flood Watch. Those living or traveling across the southwest mountains should stay weather aware through the rest of the week, and have multiple ways to receive weather warnings. As for the eastern plains, dry and continued warm conditions anticipated, though the upper ridge axis finally pushes east out of the area. Look for highs in the 60s for the high valleys, and 70s to lower 80s for the plains.

Friday...Friday will be an interesting day as the system starts to weaken and split into two pieces by the evening. The northern piece pushes up into MT, while the southern piece drops south and tries to gather some strength over the Desert SW. Rain totals of an additional .40 of an inch for the eastern San Juans, and up to a tenth of an inch elsewhere, are forecast, then showers and isolated thunderstorms push along the southern border and up across the far southeast corner through the late afternoon and evening. This will be the last really warm day for the eastern plains as temps once again climb into the 70s to around 80F, but there are some hints that perhaps it might end up a few degrees cooler due to increased cloud cover.

Saturday through Tuesday...While one low center lingers across the Four Corners, the northern piece cross the northern Rockies and pushes a cold front south into eastern CO Saturday morning. This front will bring significant cooling to the forecast area as well as widespread precipitation chances for both Sat and Sun as the southern piece of the low weakens and finally moves east across the state. Long range models indicate that Mon and Tue will remain unsettled and cool across the region, but confidence remains low on what that actually looks like. For now, the NBM drops temps into the 50s and 60s on Sat, 50s regionwide Sun and Mon, then some gradual warming by Tue.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: In the wake of this initial low, a secondary wave is forecast to dig into Arizona Saturday, before lifting into the central Rockies on Sunday.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Widespread precipitation will bring an elevated and prolonged threat of flash flooding across southern and central Utah through Thursday. There is a Slight Risk of Excessive Rainfall (level 2 of 4) across southern Utah today, and across southern through east central Utah Thursday.

- There is a slight risk (level 2 of 5) for severe thunderstorms capable of producing strong winds and hail across southern Utah Wednesday afternoon and evening, and a 2% chance of a tornado. A Marginal Risk (level 1 of 5) for severe thunderstorms is in place on Wednesday across southern and western Utah on Thursday.

- The late week storm will also bring accumulating snowfall to the high terrain across northern and central Utah on Friday, with 1-4" likely above 9000 feet. Locally higher amounts are possible in favored locations.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Midday satellite imagery and objective analysis show an upper low spinning off the CA coast, with a deep layer of southerly flow extending downstream across much of AZ and southern UT. This flow has pulled tropical moisture northward into the region, which will enhance the threat for heavy rain and flash flooding across southern and central Utah over the next 36 hours. An embedded upper jet lifting through western AZ is aiding large scale ascent, and has resulted in numerous strong to severe thunderstorms across AZ over the past few hours, while precipitation has remained more stratiform extending into south central and southeast Utah.

As the upstream low encroaches on the CA coast this afternoon through tonight, increasing upper level diffluence will spread across southern and central Utah, resulting in an increase in showers and thunderstorms. With the increase in heavy rainfall flooding is expected within most drainages across south central Utah later this afternoon through tonight. Additionally, ample deep layer shear in excess of 40 kts will support supercells capable of all severe weather hazards this afternoon and evening across southern Utah where sufficient instability exists. It appears the most likely area for severe convection will encompass far south central and southwest Utah where breaks in cloud cover are allowing surface heating and destabilization of the airmass.

As the upper low spreads inland and across the western Great Basin Thursday, increasing large scale forcing will maintain showers and thunderstorms across southern and central Utah, with this activity spreading into northern Utah during the afternoon and evening hours. Ample deep layer shear will continue to support organized convection anywhere sufficient instability can develop through Thursday evening, particularly across southern and western Utah.

As the upper low quickly lifts through northern Utah into southern Idaho Thursday night into Friday, precipitation will wind down from south to north with time. Colder air being pulled into the area as this low passes will drop snow levels into the 8000-8500 foot range across northern Utah. Accumulating snow is still expected across the northern mountains above 9000 feet, however the overall evolution of the pattern and shorter duration of precipitation will likely keep accumulation limited to the 1-4" range, with a few pockets of higher amounts possible.

In the wake of this initial low, a secondary wave is forecast to dig into Arizona Saturday, before lifting into the central Rockies on Sunday. This will maintain cool temperatures through the weekend, with precipitation persisting across eastern portions of the forecast area. Beyond the weekend, drier conditions with seasonal temperatures are expected, however confidence is low in how the large scale pattern will evolve through next week.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Brian Lazar
bottom_line: Colorado is in store for some healthy moisture in the final week and half of October. This will mostly be rain during the week, with snowlines rising above 12,000 feet. For areas with snow on the ground, favoring the San Juan Mountains, this means rain on snow and the potential for Wet Loose avalanches.

Cooler temperatures arrive for the weekend with snow levels dropping to 10,000 feet or lower. This will allow snow to start accumulating in most mountain areas. The San Juan Mountains could see a foot of accumulation by late Sunday at the higher elevations. The Central Mountains could see as much as 6 or 7 inches, with half that further north.

It's time to start thinking about avalanches on steep, snow-covered slopes. Once snow piles up or drifts deep enough to obscure the ground cover, avalanches are possible. This doesn't take much on grassy slopes or steep rock slabs or permanent snowfields.
Nearly every fall, avalanches catch eager riders and late-season hikers off guard. Hunters traveling through the high country need to exercise caution on steep, snow-covered terrain.
We will update the Statewide Avalanche Conditions as necessary. On November 1, 2026, we will resume our daily weather and avalanche forecasts.
We will update the Field Report and Avalanche Observations as information comes in, so please send us your observations.

You can get up-to-date point weather forecasts on our Weather Forecasts page by clicking on the map or searching for a location. You can also get model forecasts on our Point Forecasts page and Model Forecast page. You can check current weather conditions across Colorado on our Weather Stations page.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.
Seasonal SNOW AND PRECIPITATION Comparison
(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
• November - 5" (4" SWE)
• December - 68" (12.6" SWE)
• January - 37" (5.1" SWE)
• February - 41" (5.4" SWE)
• March - 24" (5.2" SWE) Peak Height of Snow - 70" (03/05)
• November - 70" (10" SWE)
• December- 61" (6.9" SWE)
• January- 34" (4.3" SWE)
• February- 74" (11.4" SWE)
• March - 57" (7.5" SWE) Peak Height of Snow- 112" (03/17)
